1:
Henry and Ellicott catch the same overtone in "full of days". Henry renders it satur dierum, satisfied with living in this world, and notes that David was but seventy when he died; Gill guesses the last year of his age. Ellicott takes it literally as satisfied with days, suspects our pointing may be wrong, and reaches for Horace, who describes the philosopher departing this life like a satisfied guest. On what follows the two divide by method rather than by judgment. Ellicott observes that the bare statement that David made Solomon king is all the chronicler repeats from the opening of Kings, a narrative intimately connected with David's family affairs, with which he is not concerned to deal. Henry supplies exactly what Ellicott says has been withheld, insisting that Solomon was made king to reign after his father, not with him or under him, and that doing it in a solemn assembly of all the princes made Adonijah's later attempt the more impudent and ridiculous.

The assembly itself Ellicott treats constitutionally: the princes, the priests and the Levites are in the chronicler's conception the three estates of the realm, representatives of all spiritual and temporal authority, so David consults the national assembly in a matter of national concern. Delitzsch says the same, that the numbering was a matter of national importance and the princes stood for the lay tribes. Henry alone notices the shadow of the earlier census: Joab had not numbered the Levites, and David numbers them now, but not in pride, and so need not fear wrath for it.

Verse 3 raises two problems and no commentator handles both. Its upper limit is missing, and Clarke and Wesley account for that the same way: the fifty-year cap in the wilderness existed because the Levites carried the tabernacle and sacred vessels, and with the ark fixed that reason wholly ceased, so even an old man might continue to serve. Its lower limit conflicts with verse 24, and Delitzsch attacks it: Moses himself at a later time set the age at twenty-five, verse 24 distinctly says twenty and grounds the change on the nature of the service, and the later books agree, so it is not probable that David confined the numbering to thirty and upward. Ellicott passes over both difficulties and parses the idiom instead: "by their polls, man by man" is literally by their skulls, by men, the second phrase defining the first so as to exclude women and children. Henry does the arithmetic: 8,580 serviceable Levites in the wilderness against 38,000 now, an increase far beyond the proportion of the other tribes.

Delitzsch and Ellicott then converge independently on a point of punctuation. Because verse 5 says "the instruments which I made", both conclude that verses 4 and 5 are David's own words and must be read as a spoken decree, Delitzsch supplying "and David said" before verse 4, Ellicott putting the whole in inverted commas and rendering the numbers as a command. Ellicott mentions but sets aside the alternative, that the narrative is interrupted by a fragment of an old poem spoken in God's name.

On those instruments Clarke and Ellicott cite the same verse of Amos to opposite ends. Ellicott takes the prophet's gibe at nobles who invent themselves instruments of music like David as proof that David was not only a minstrel and inspired psalmist but an inventor of stringed instruments. Clarke reads the same parallel as a condemnation of the instruments, and goes further: David made this distribution according to his own judgment and from the dictates of his piety, but it does not appear he had any positive divine authority for such arrangements. Henry, untroubled, finds the whole establishment fitting, since much of the state of great men consists in the greatness of their retinue, and remarks that of all men an idle Levite makes the worst figure.
7:
Delitzsch sets out the principle behind the list. In the natural development of Israel the sons of Jacob founded the tribes, their sons the families, and their grandsons the fathers'-houses; but the scheme was never carried through consistently, partly because some lines were not numerous enough to form independent houses and partly because houses that had decreased were attached to others. The chapter shows both at work: two of Shimei's four sons, Jeush and Beriah, had not many sons, so they were reckoned as one house and one muster. Clarke gives the merger a practical reason, that two small families together might do work too much for either separately; Henry gives it a moral one, that those weak and little separately may be put together and appear considerable.

Ellicott turns the genealogy into an arithmetical problem. The Levitical courses, he argues, were twenty-four like those of the musicians and the priests, as Josephus states, and at a thousand to the class that tallies exactly with the twenty-four thousand overseers. Gershon supplies nine houses and Kohath nine, so Merari must supply six; but the text as it stands yields only four. A later chapter names a third son of Merari with three houses, which would give seven, one too many. Ellicott strikes the second Mahli of verse 23 as an ancient scribe's repetition of the Mahli of verse 21, the closing "three" added after the mistake set. He then lists the evidence against himself: the later passage itself needs emendation, all the old versions support the present text so the assumed omission must be very ancient, the two other places naming Merari's sons give only two, and the recurrence of a name within a family is easily paralleled in this chapter.

Delitzsch moves the opposite way. Where Ellicott treats the later chapter as sound and emends this one, Delitzsch calls the conclusion that Merari really had a third son whose name has dropped out simply incorrect, on the ground that the verses supplying that third son are recognisable from their whole character as arbitrary interpolations. The two agree on nothing except that the text will not balance as it stands.

Smaller identifications turn on the same crowding of names. Gill, following Kimchi, distinguishes the Shimei of verse 9, a descendant of Laadan, from the Shimei of verse 10, Gershon's own son and Laadan's brother; Ellicott makes the same distinction and notes that one name is spelt Zina in one verse and Zizah in the next, preferring the second. He separates Gershom, which means expulsion and is a variant of Gershon, from the allusive play made on it in Exodus, and Eliezer from Eleazar. On Eleazar's daughters Clarke and Ellicott agree, both appealing to the law made for the daughters of Zelophehad, that heiresses marry within their father's tribe so the estate is not alienated; Delitzsch adds that Mahli's line was thereby comprehended in the single house of Kish.

The separation of Aaron draws Ellicott's closest reading. The clause is not that Aaron should sanctify the most holy things but that he should be hallowed as most holy, an expression applied to him nowhere else in Scripture, marking the priests as a higher grade of holiness called to a holier ministry; and the verb rendered "burn incense" covers burning victims as well. Clarke keeps to the plain sense of the last clause: the blessing is pronounced over the people by invoking the name of the Lord. Henry draws the moral: the posterity of Moses stands level with the common Levites while Aaron's is advanced to the priesthood, which he reads as evidence of Moses's self-denial and the recompense of Aaron's, since those content to stoop are in the fairest way to rise. Clarke supplies the Targum's version of the same idea: on account of the merits of Moses the posterity of Rehabiah were multiplied to more than sixty myriads.
24:
Verse 24 numbers the Levites from twenty where verse 3 numbered them from thirty, and the chapter's difficulty turns on it. Ellicott surveys the options without settling on one: some would banish the discrepancy by taking "thirty" for an ancient error of transcription, others suppose the chronicler simply incorporated two divergent statements, and the older commentators held that David numbered twice, first from thirty as the Law required and again towards the close of his reign from twenty, the duties having become less onerous. He then undercuts the last by noting that twenty was in any case the military age. Clarke takes the two-decrees view flatly: this was a different ordinance, these were David's last orders, and they should begin earlier and continue later. Wesley proposes that both ages stood at once, twenty being when a Levite was solemnly prepared, instructed and by degrees exercised in some parts of the work, and thirty the age of full admission to his office. Henry supplies a motive none of the others considers: the young Levites, having no work till they were older, may have got a habit of idleness or grown addicted to their pleasures, a blemish to their reputation and a hindrance to their usefulness afterwards, which setting them to work at twenty prevented.

The reason the text itself gives is the ark's rest. Ellicott renders verse 25 not "that they may dwell" but "and He hath settled in Jerusalem for ever", Zion being now chosen as the eternal dwelling-place, and observes that the older service was heavier not only because the Levites carried the sacred dwelling about but because they had to guard it against marauders. Henry reaches the same conclusion from providence rather than philology: God considers our frame, and in service as well as sufferings will lay no more upon us than we are able to bear. Both he and Wesley add a second reason, that the people were now multiplied and more hands needed, so every Israelite who brought an offering might find a Levite ready to assist him.

Ellicott takes verse 27 for a parenthetic remark of the chronicler, interrupting a speech of David's that resumes at the next verse.

On the Levites' charge of measures the commentators part. Clarke, Wesley and Henry all make them custodians of the national standards, kept in the sanctuary, by which the weights and measures of the land were tried when appealed to. Ellicott confines it to the sanctuary's own use: the flour, wine and oil that were the complements of every sacrifice were measured in standard vessels the Levites kept, one Hebrew word meaning capacity and the other length. Clarke dismisses as a conceit the tradition that the priests themselves sowed, ground and baked the grain for the shewbread.

Delitzsch and Ellicott agree that the morning and evening thanksgiving belongs to the singers and not to the Levites who assisted at the altar; Delitzsch says the contrary opinion needs no serious refutation, since we can hardly believe psalms were sung while the beasts were slaughtered and skinned; Ellicott puts it more mildly, that those who slew and flayed the victims could hardly have taken part in the service of song. Gill, following the Targum and Kimchi, resolves it differently, holding that the Levites sang whenever burnt offerings were brought, while some of them helped the priests in slaying the sacrifices. Henry adds that Moses appointed trumpets over the burnt offerings, a sound awful and affecting but not articulate, and not so reasonable a service as the psalms David appointed. At the close Clarke stresses subordination, the Levites being properly servants to the priests, employed about the more servile part of worship; Henry stresses the check on it, the priests being called their brethren to remind them they were hewn out of the same rock and must not lord it over them.
